The Knowledge Gap

Experts lamented the think tank's closures as a significant loss for policymakers, advocates, and researchers who have relied on the data to prevent shootings.

Share

The RAND Corporation is sunsetting two major gun violence research initiatives as funding has shrunk under the Trump administration. Experts lamented the closures as a significant loss for policymakers, advocates, and researchers who have relied on the think tank’s work to prevent shootings.

The Gun Policy in America project, an initiative that evaluated how researchers conducted their studies and what they found, concluded with a final update to its Science of Gun Policy report on January 29, Andrew Morral, a RAND senior behavioral scientist who co-led the project, told The Trace. The project provided what experts called the most sweeping and reliable synthesis of evidence on the effectiveness of various gun laws, from background checks on gun sales to assault weapons bans.

Another RAND initiative, the National Collaborative on Gun Violence Research, which has poured at least $24 million into gun violence research since 2018, is also ending. In November, the collaborative awarded grants to three post-doctoral researchers examining Extreme Risk Protection Order laws, or red flag laws, which allow courts to temporarily disarm people deemed dangerous. The awards were likely the initiative’s last, said Morral, who also directs the collaborative.

Charles Branas, a Columbia University epidemiologist and prominent gun violence researcher, said the closures leave a significant void. He lauded the Gun Policy in America project as “almost indispensable,” as it mapped the methods researchers were using and developed recommendations so the field could study state gun laws more consistently.

He said the project also functioned as an “evidence and gap map,” laying out the full landscape of gun laws and their outcomes in a way that highlighted where evidence was missing entirely. “It’s so instructive to find out where we don’t know anything,” Branas said.

Morral blamed the closures on a combination of factors. With the Trump administration slashing federal funding for research on gun violence, health care, climate, and other issues, major philanthropies that funded work like RAND’s have been stretched thin as competition for their money increases. Some have also grown reluctant to support gun violence research amid a more hostile political environment. “Research on gun policy has always been very third-rail-ish,” Morral said. “There are very few willing to wade into the trouble they might face for supporting research on this topic.”

RAND ran a research portfolio much broader than gun violence. While the gun research didn’t rely on federal funding, the rest of the organization did. In October, the federal cuts forced RAND to lay off nearly 200 people. “All these things combine to make it a tough environment to continue working in this area,” Morral said.

Journalists and advocates frequently cited the organization’s work. Rosanna Smart, a RAND senior economist who co-led the Gun Policy in America project with Morral, said it was rewarding seeing how useful the work was to people outside academia. “Hearing from journalists, people who work for federal and state agencies, and people who are not engaged in research but consume it, has been a real highlight for me,” she said.

The project maintained databases of state gun laws, along with estimates of household firearm ownership and shooting-related hospitalizations. Researchers from a wide range of disciplines have used those resources to support dozens of studies, making RAND’s work a backbone for much of the field.

Branas said RAND’s National Collaborative did a lot to support researchers early in their careers. “These are people who could have gone on and studied anything,” he said. “They chose this because they saw it as a legitimate career path — and the collaborative was part of it.” Losing that funding could mean fewer researchers in the long run.

Trace public health reporter Fairriona Magee contributed reporting to this story.

Before joining The Trace as an investigative fellow in June 2020, Chip worked as a reporter and the editor-in-chief of his collegiate newspaper, The Auburn Plainsman. He also covered the state legislature, governor, courts, and elections for the Alabama Political Reporter. As an undergraduate, Chip studied political science and journalism at Auburn University. He also earned an M.A. with a concentration in politics from the Columbia Journalism School.
